segments.title: Why the Leanders sit awkwardly between cruiser roles
segments.body: The Leanders are attractive ships, and the criticism here concerns their fit within the light-cruiser category. By the 1930s, the light-cruiser category had absorbed duties formerly divided among first- and second-class protected cruisers and scout cruisers. A design assessed against that combined category can appear weak at either end because it was built for something in between. In this reading, the Leanders make more sense as the equivalent of second-class protected cruisers than as pure scouts or first-class protected cruisers.

evidence.note: The opening praises the ships before explaining the criticism of their role. The Leanders are interpreted as a second-class protected-cruiser concept between scout and first-class roles.

segments.summary: The Leanders occupy the space between scout cruisers and first-class protected cruisers, so broad light-cruiser comparisons make their role look awkward.

segments.title: Why the Leander retains an older cruiser role
segments.body: A Leander would have filled the old second-class protected-cruiser role exceptionally well if that category had continued into the 1930s. The formal role had disappeared, but the designers and admirals behind the new cruisers had learned their trade while it still existed. Their professional habits could survive the change in labels. That earlier experience helps explain the Leander's intermediate position among newer light cruisers.

evidence.note: The Leander is assessed as an exceptional 1930s equivalent of the old second-class protected cruiser. The role no longer officially existed, but designers and admirals had learned their trade when it did.

segments.summary: The Leander is an excellent fit for the old second-class protected-cruiser role in this interpretation, even though that formal category had disappeared by the 1930s.

segments.title: The Leander as a starting point for a cruiser programme
segments.body: A middle-of-the-road design offers a sensible starting point for reviving a light-cruiser programme. The Leander could theoretically provide a base from which to develop ships for either end of the role spectrum. Enlarging the concept could lead toward a Town-class cruiser comparable to a first-class protected cruiser. Reducing it could produce a scout-cruiser type, with Arethusa offered as the closer comparison rather than Amphion.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the Leander a sensible base that could theoretically be enlarged toward the Town class or reduced toward a scout cruiser. The caption 'refuser' is understood as Arethusa in the comparison with Amphion.

segments.summary: A middle-of-the-road Leander could theoretically provide a basis for developing larger Town-type cruisers or smaller scouts closer to Arethusa.
